### [1:40–3:00] MISTAKE 1 — AUTOMATING A BROKEN PROCESS
**NARRATION:** "Mistake one, and it's the most common: automating a process that's already
broken. If your intake form asks the wrong questions, or your follow-up email confuses people,
automating it doesn't fix that — it just sends the mess faster, to more people, forever. The fix
is boring and it works: run the process by hand a few times first, clean it up, then automate the
version that actually works. Gut-check question one — 'Would I be happy if this ran a thousand
times exactly as it is today?' If the honest answer's no, don't automate it yet."
**[VISUAL]:** A messy paper form → photocopier spitting out 500 messy copies → hard cut to a
clean form, then automated. **[TAKEAWAY on screen]:** "Fix the process first. Then automate it."
**[QUOTABLE]:** "Automating a broken process doesn't fix it — it just breaks it faster, at scale."

### [3:00–4:15] MISTAKE 2 — NO HUMAN HANDOFF
**NARRATION:** "Mistake two: no human handoff. You set up a chatbot or an auto-reply, and then a
customer asks something weird — a refund, a complaint, an angry message — and the automation just
keeps cheerfully answering wrong. That's how you lose people. The fix is an escape hatch: a rule
that says 'when you hit something outside the script, stop and pass it to a human.' Every good
automation has one. Gut-check question two — 'When this hits something it can't handle, where does
it send it?' If you don't have an answer, that's your next job."
**[VISUAL]:** Chatbot happily giving a wrong answer to an upset customer → then a clean "handoff to
human" flag lights up and a person steps in. **[TAKEAWAY on screen]:** "Build the escape hatch:
weird stuff goes to a human."
**[QUOTABLE]:** "Every automation needs an escape hatch — a moment where a human takes over."

### [5:00–6:10] MISTAKE 3 — OVER-AUTOMATING TOO FAST
**NARRATION:** "Mistake three: over-automating too fast. You watch a video like this, get
excited, and wire up ten automations in one weekend. Then something breaks and you have no idea
which one — because you can't see where the problem started. The fix is patience you can actually
stick to: turn on one automation, watch it for a week, make sure it behaves, then add the next.
Slower start, way fewer fires. Gut-check question three — 'Am I turning on one thing right now, or
ten?'"
**[VISUAL]:** A tangle of ten wires all sparking at once → rewind → one clean wire, a calendar
marking a week, then a second wire added. **[TAKEAWAY on screen]:** "One automation. Watch a week.
Then the next."
**[QUOTABLE]:** "Automate one thing, watch it for a week, then add the next — speed is how
automations go wrong quietly."

### [6:10–7:20] MISTAKE 4 — IGNORING DATA PRIVACY
**NARRATION:** "Mistake four: ignoring data privacy. When you automate, you're handing customer
info — names, emails, maybe payment details — to software. If you never check where that data goes
or who can see it, you're taking a risk that's cheap to avoid. The fix isn't complicated: before
you connect a tool, ask what customer data it touches, where that data is stored, and whether it
gets used to train anything. Pick tools that let you say no to that. Gut-check question four —
'What customer data is this touching, and where does it go?'"
**[VISUAL]:** A customer's info flowing into a tool → a simple checklist stamps "What data? ·
Stored where? · Used to train?" **[TAKEAWAY on screen]:** "Know what data each tool touches —
before you connect it."
**[QUOTABLE]:** "If you don't know where your customer data goes, you've already made the fourth
mistake."

### [7:20–8:30] MISTAKE 5 — NO ROI CHECK (the sleeper)
**NARRATION:** "And mistake five, the one almost nobody catches: no ROI check. You set up an
automation, it feels productive, and you just… never look at whether it actually saved time or
made money. Months later you're paying for five tools and you couldn't tell me which ones earn
their keep. The fix takes five minutes: before you turn something on, write down what you expect —
hours saved, or dollars — and put a reminder to check in thirty days. If it didn't pay off, kill
it. That's the loop I promised you'd want at the end."
**[VISUAL]:** A pile of subscription logos → a simple two-column check "Expected vs Actual" →
